question_text: A 6-month-old baby boy presents to his pediatrician for the evaluation of recurrent bacterial infections. He is currently well but has already been hospitalized multiple times due to his bacterial infections. His blood pressure is 103/67 mm Hg and heart rate is 74/min. Physical examination reveals light-colored skin and silver hair. On examination of a peripheral blood smear, large cytoplasmic vacuoles containing microbes are found within the neutrophils. What diagnosis do these findings suggest?

                    ### Question
                    A 6-month-old baby boy presents to his pediatrician for the evaluation of recurrent bacterial infections. He is currently well but has already been hospitalized multiple times due to his bacterial infections. His blood pressure is 103/67 mm Hg and heart rate is 74/min. Physical examination reveals light-colored skin and silver hair. On examination of a peripheral blood smear, large cytoplasmic vacuoles containing microbes are found within the neutrophils. What diagnosis do these findings suggest?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Chediak-Higashi syndrome
opb. Leukocyte adhesion deficiency-1
opc. Congenital thymic aplasia
opd. Common variable immunodeficiency
ope. Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The clinical presentation of recurrent bacterial infections, light-colored skin, silver hair, and the presence of large cytoplasmic vacuoles in neutrophils strongly suggests Chediak-Higashi syndrome. This condition is characterized by a defect in lysosomal trafficking due to mutations in the LYST gene, leading to impaired neutrophil function and partial oculocutaneous albinism. The retrieved evidence paths, while broad, support the involvement of neutrophils and genetic factors in Chediak-Higashi syndrome. Other options, such as leukocyte adhesion deficiency-1, congenital thymic aplasia, common variable immunodeficiency, and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, do not align with the specific combination of symptoms and blood smear findings presented in this case. Therefore, the most likely diagnosis is Chediak-Higashi syndrome.
